items.title: Nabis June 2026 California and New York Cannabis Policy Updates
items.summary: California and New York are tightening cannabis regulations in June 2026 across packaging, labeling, and supply chain compliance. In California, AB 2532 caps cannabis beverage servings at 10 mg THC and requires the national Poison Help line on all edible and beverage labels, likely taking effect July 1, 2027. AB 2249 bans cannabis packaging attractive to children — including cartoons, anthropomorphic characters, and certain font styles — and requires the Department of Cannabis Control to publish a compliance rubric by July 1, 2027, with sales allowed through January 1, 2028. In New York, lawmakers passed A10698, the Cannabis Supply Chain Integrity and Anti-Inversion Act, on June 2, 2026, defining and penalizing "cannabis inversion" — the introduction of illicit cannabis into the licensed supply chain — with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day and a rebuttable presumption of license revocation for labs that submit fraudulent certificates of analysis. Separately, California's SB 54 required cannabis operators to register with CalRecycle as a Producer by June 1, 2026, ahead of a 2032 deadline for recyclable or compostable packaging. Here's what licensed operators need to know about each bill and what to do now.

items.title: Federal Cannabis Reform in 2026: Why Industry Leaders Call It a Tailwind, Not a Lifeline
items.summary: Federal cannabis reform in 2026 is gaining measurable momentum, but industry leaders caution that rescheduling and safe banking are not immediate solutions for operators. At IgniteIt’s New Jersey Spotlight panel, Nabis CEO Vince C. Ning joined capital markets and policy experts to break down what federal cannabis rescheduling, safe banking legislation, hemp regulation, and interstate commerce could realistically mean for licensed operators. While the potential shift from Schedule I to Schedule III could ease 280E tax burdens, panelists emphasized that regulatory clarity, IRS interpretation, and implementation timelines will determine real impact. Discussions also highlighted how federal cannabis policy is evolving from plant-based frameworks toward cannabinoid-centric regulation, signaling structural change across compliance, packaging, and interstate distribution. The takeaway: federal cannabis reform represents a long-term tailwind for the industry, not a short-term lifeline. For operators navigating compliance risk, capital constraints, and market volatility, disciplined fundamentals remain essential as Washington’s policy landscape continues to evolve.

items.title: February 2026 California and New York and Cannabis Policy Updates
items.summary: February 2026 brought significant cannabis policy updates in both California and New York, with implications for licensed dispensaries, distributors, beverage manufacturers, and multi-state operators. California’s proposed AB 1826 would refine recall, embargo, and product destruction procedures, directly affecting compliance workflows and inventory risk management. In New York, lawmakers enacted a zoning fix protecting more than 150 licensed dispensaries from closure, while a newly introduced bill (A10191) proposes allowing liquor and wine stores to sell low-potency (≤5mg THC) cannabis beverages under a new retail permit structure. Together, these developments signal continued regulatory evolution in mature and emerging cannabis markets, reinforcing the importance of legislative monitoring for operators navigating compliance, retail expansion, and beverage distribution strategy in 2026.
